question: to the Commission Sakis Arnaoutoglou (S&D) Subject:
Shortcomings in the implementation of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 by Greek administrative and consular authorities

Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 was introduced with the aim of facilitating the free movement of citizens within the EU by abolishing legalisation or apostille requirements for certain public civil status documents, introducing multilingual standard forms and simplifying translation procedures. Greek citizens residing or active in other Member States have reported that Greek administrative or consular authorities are still demanding apostilles, certified translations or other additional paperwork. This entails financial cost, loss of working time and possible cases of unequal treatment. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.

Has it verified to what extent Greece has implemented Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 with regard to ending the legalisation/apostille requirement for certain civil status documents, the mandatory acceptance of the multilingual standard forms provided for in the regulation and the envisaged translation arrangements?
If shortcomings have been identified, what specific infringements, administrative practices or differences in interpretation has it recorded, and what corrective measures does it intend to take?

In addition, has it examined whether the current practices of Greek consular or internal administrative authorities – such as demanding apostilles, certified translations or other additional paperwork – result in disproportionate costs, delays or discriminatory treatment between married parents whose marriage has already been registered in Greece, married parents whose marriage was performed abroad but has not yet been registered and unmarried parents and, if so, does it consider that such differentiation constitutes a possible breach of EU law requiring further action?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) Regulation (EU) 2016/11911 aims to facilitate the free movement of citizens within the EU by abolishing legalisation or apostille requirements for certain public civil status documents, introducing multilingual standard forms and simplifying translation procedures. The Regulation is an important piece of legislation cutting red tape and costs for citizens, when they need to present in a Member State a public document issued in another Member State. The Commission monitors the correct application of EU legislation by Member States and may decide to take appropriate actions in cases showing a persistent failure by a Member State to apply EU law correctly. In the case of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191, there are no concrete indications of such infringements by Greece to the knowledge of the Commission. If evidence comes to light of a practice of Greek administrative or consular authorities demanding apostilles, certified translations or other additional paperwork in violation of the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/1191 on a general and consistent basis, the Commission would, where appropriate, take the necessary steps. Citizens who encounter problems which are allegedly caused by the misapplication of the Regulation by Greece can file a complaint to the Commission providing details of the alleged breach. On this basis the Commission is able to examine the matter and contact Greece if needed. The Commission is not able to examine the alleged breach on the basis of a general statement but would need further details.
